newsitem.title: UK: Booming UK services magnifies calls for rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Booming UK services magnifies calls for rate rise.

text.p: Expectations of higher British interest rates mounted again on Thursday after another batch of data suggested the economy is roaring ahead.
A new survey from the Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply showed the service sector, which makes up around two thirds of the economy, was booming.

It said services output, new and outstanding business, employment and prices all rose in March. Output had risen in every month since July, the first month for which figures were available, and accelerated sharply last month.
"There is more than enough evidence to suggest the economy is growing too strongly," said Goldman Sachs UK economist David Walton.
"Interest rates need to rise by somewhere between 100 and 150 basis points over the next twelve months," he said.

Analysts say whichever party wins the May 1 election will have to raise interest rates immediately by around 1/2 point from their current level of 6.0 percent if the economy is to be prevented from overheating.

Financial markets are taking a particularly hawkish attitude on the need to raise rates with sterling underpinned by the speculation and short sterling futures -- a gauge of interest rates sentiment -- looking for rates of over 6.5 percent by the end of June and seven percent by the end of the year.
The new CIPS services sector survey showed the overall business activity index stood at a seasonally adjusted 63.3 compared with 60.4 in February and 56.6 last July.

Analysts said the survey would be more useful once it had established a track record but it did seem to confirm the buoyancy of service sector demand and suggested both prices and wages were creeping higher.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke seized the survey data as evidence that his policies were working. "Britain's service sector is booming. Employment is rising and most firms expect business to increase over the next year," he said.
"We must keep in place for the next five years the policies and stable economic conditions which have enabled Britain's service industries to do so well."
The Conservatives argue the economy has escaped from the old boom/bust cycle and is now in a controlled boom, with no sign of inflation pressures and with the strength of sterling providing a brake.
Royal Bank of Scotland economist Marion Bell argues that if the Conservatives confound the pollsters and win the election, Clarke will not raise rates.
"If Clarke is Chancellor again, I don't think rates will go up. He can't fight an election campaign saying rates don't need to rise and then put them up straight afterwards," she said.
"I think he believes his own rhetoric," she said.

Clarke has already refused several Bank of England requests for rates to rise. The central bank has said that the UK has little chance of hitting its target of 2.5 percent inflation without higher interest rates.
By contrast, the opposition Labour Party which is widely expected to seize power and is desperate to show it is not soft on inflation, would be putty in the central bank's hands.
"A Labour Chancellor will do whatever the Bank wants and can blame it on the previous government," Bell said.
The Confederation of Britsh Industry's March distributive trades survey, also published on Thursday, further reinforced the picture of strength in the service sector.
The three month trend showed the slowdown in the pace of growth has levelled off and shopkeepers say business is above average for the time of year.
But HSBC economist Jonathan Loynes said the weakness of the manufacturing sector means that a fiscal tightening would be far more effective than a monetary tightening.
"It looks to me as if the economy needs slowing down, but our advice would be to do it on the fiscal side to cool down the consumer."
He said an interest rate rise would also serve to drive the pound up further, hurting manufacturers.
